question: to the Commission Pascal Arimont (PPE) Subject:

Research is ongoing under the Interreg EDEN-Medical project1 on the cross-border use of drones in medical logistics, for instance for transporting medicines, laboratory samples or medical equipment between hospitals. A recent study by the Institute for Transnational and Euregional cross-border cooperation and Mobility2 highlights major legal and administrative obstacles, including separate authorisation procedures in a number of Member States, divergent national aviation practices, an absence of harmonised geo-zones, outstanding issues in operations beyond the visual line of sight (BVLOS) and ad hoc operations, liability, insurance, health data and reimbursement. 1.
Is the Commission planning legislative or other measures to facilitate cross-border drone flights for medical logistics, as well as for fire brigades and other emergency services?
Will the Commission consider introducing a uniform application procedure or mutual recognition of national authorisations for cross-border drone operations, particularly in border regions?

How does the Commission intend to integrate the lessons learned from the EDENMedical project into its work on crisis preparedness, civil protection, digital health and advanced air mobility solutions?
https://www.interregmeuserhine.eu/en/projects/eden-medical/ https://crossborderitem.eu/wp-content/uploads/EDEN-Medical-Concept-Paper-1.pdf
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) The EU regulatory framework for Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) is based on an operationcentric and risk-based approach, allowing operations to be authorised according to their level of risk. This framework already enables UAS beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) operations, including medical logistics use cases, to the extent these operations are not excluded from European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) Basic Regulation coverage (Regulation (EU) 2018/11391) and its implementing rules as provided by Article 2(3)(a). The need for separate authorisation procedures in each Member State is largely due to the diverging approaches used to assess and mitigate air risk. As part of the continuous regulatory monitoring and review process, EASA has proposed an amendment to the U-space framework that aims to establish common procedures to address the lack of mutual recognition of operational authorisations among the different Member States. The Commission will continue to assess whether further action is needed in the context of the implementation of the EU drone framework, the roll-out of the U-space framework, and the follow-up to the Drone Strategy 2.0. As regards a uniform application procedure or mutual recognition of national authorisations, the Commission will continue, with EASA and Member States, to encourage convergence in administrative practices, facilitate the exchange of lessons learned including EU funded projects and to identify whether additional measures could further simplify cross-border procedures, while preserving safety oversight, responsibilities and sovereignty of national competent authorities.
